blocks.text: A complete ear examination assesses the external ear, external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, middle ear, hearing, and vestibular function when indicated. It also includes examination of the surrounding structures, particularly the mastoid region, cranial nerves and upper respiratory tract.

The aim is not merely to identify ear abnormalities. You should be able to perform each manoeuvre correctly, explain what it tests, interpret abnormal findings, recognise emergencies, and present your findings in a structured OSCE format.
Otoscope
Used to inspect the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane.
512 Hz tuning fork
Used for Rinne and Weber tests to help distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss.
Audiometer and headphones
Used for formal hearing threshold assessment when available.
Pen torch
Useful for inspecting the pinna, external ear and surrounding structures.
Other useful equipment includes disposable gloves when indicated, an appropriate speculum, a tuning fork of another frequency if required, and equipment for assessing balance or vestibular function.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity and explain the examination.
Obtain consent and ask about pain before touching the ear.
Ask whether the patient has hearing aids and whether they can be removed comfortably.
Position the patient sitting upright, with adequate lighting.
Examine both ears, even if symptoms affect only one side.
Ask about previous ear surgery, perforation, ear tubes, trauma and discharge before performing any manoeuvre that might cause discomfort or risk injury.

blocks.text: Safety point: Do not irrigate an ear if tympanic membrane perforation is suspected, there is a history of relevant ear surgery without appropriate assessment, or another contraindication is present. Avoid inserting instruments blindly into the canal.
A focused history helps you decide which parts of the examination deserve particular attention.

items.text: When did the pain begin?
Is it sudden or gradual?
Is it constant or intermittent?
Is it unilateral or bilateral?
Is the pain severe, dull, sharp or throbbing?
Is it worsened by pulling the pinna, pressing the tragus, chewing or swallowing?
Is there fever, discharge or hearing loss?
Pain on tragal pressure or movement of the pinna suggests otitis externa.
Deep ear pain with fever or preceding upper respiratory symptoms may suggest acute otitis media.
Ear pain with a normal ear examination may be referred from dental disease, the temporomandibular joint, pharynx or larynx.
Severe persistent otalgia in a patient with diabetes or immunosuppression raises concern for necrotising otitis externa.
Duration and frequency.
Amount and colour.
Whether it is watery, purulent, bloody or foul-smelling.
Whether it is associated with pain or fever.
Previous episodes and treatment.

blocks.text: Foul-smelling chronic discharge may occur with chronic suppurative otitis media or cholesteatoma. Blood-stained discharge can occur after trauma or infection, but also requires assessment for other causes.
Important: Clear fluid or blood from the ear after significant head trauma may indicate a serious injury, including a cerebrospinal fluid leak or temporal bone fracture.

items.text: Sudden or gradual onset.
One ear or both.
Difficulty hearing conversations, speech in noise or telephone calls.
Associated tinnitus, vertigo, pain or discharge.
Previous exposure to loud noise.
Ear infections, trauma and ototoxic medication exposure.
Family history of hearing loss.

blocks.text: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss developing over hours to a few days is an otological emergency. Do not delay urgent assessment while attempting to remove wax or complete routine testing.
Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external sound source.

items.text: Unilateral or bilateral.
Continuous or intermittent.
Pulsatile or non-pulsatile.
Associated with hearing loss, vertigo, neurological symptoms or medication exposure.

blocks.text: Unilateral persistent tinnitus and pulsatile tinnitus warrant appropriate clinical investigation. Tinnitus associated with sudden hearing loss or acute neurological symptoms requires urgent assessment.

items.text: Is there a spinning sensation or general light-headedness?
Is it triggered by head movement?
How long does each episode last?
Is there nausea or vomiting?
Is there hearing loss or tinnitus?
Are there headache, double vision, weakness, numbness or difficulty walking?

blocks.text: Brief, position-triggered episodes may suggest benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Prolonged vertigo may occur in vestibular neuritis or other vestibular disorders, while vertigo with hearing symptoms may indicate labyrinthine or other inner-ear pathology.
However, new severe vertigo with neurological symptoms, inability to walk, or other concerning signs may indicate a central cause, including stroke.
Begin by inspecting both ears from the front, side and behind. Compare the two sides for symmetry and abnormalities.

items.text: Helix and antihelix.
Tragus and antitragus.
Concha.
External auditory meatus.
Earlobe.
Surrounding skin.
Congenital abnormalities or low-set ears.
Swelling, redness or tenderness.
Skin lesions, ulcers, scars or deformities.
Trauma, lacerations or bruising.
Discharge at the meatus.
Preauricular sinuses, pits or tags.
Evidence of previous surgery or hearing devices.

content_groups.group_title: B. Clinical significance of external ear abnormalities

blocks.text: Auricular haematoma

Blood collects between the auricular cartilage and its perichondrium, commonly after blunt trauma. The pinna becomes swollen and may lose its normal contours. Prompt assessment is needed to prevent cartilage damage and cauliflower ear.
Perichondritis
Painful, red swelling of the cartilaginous pinna, often sparing the soft earlobe. It may follow trauma, piercing or infection and requires prompt treatment.
Preauricular sinus
A small congenital opening, usually anterior to the upper part of the pinna. It may be asymptomatic or become infected.

content_groups.group_title: C. Palpate the pinna and tragus

blocks.text: Gently palpate the pinna and press the tragus.
Ask the patient whether this produces pain.

items.text: Marked pain on tragal pressure or movement of the pinna is characteristic of otitis externa.
Pain may also occur with trauma, perichondritis or other local inflammatory conditions.
Absence of tragal tenderness does not exclude ear infection.

blocks.text: Do not manipulate an injured ear unnecessarily.
Inspect the area behind each ear for swelling, redness, scars and displacement of the pinna.
Palpate the mastoid process gently for tenderness.

Mastoiditis should be suspected when there is postauricular redness, swelling and tenderness, particularly with fever or recent acute otitis media. The pinna may protrude or be pushed forwards and downwards.
This requires urgent hospital assessment because infection can spread to surrounding structures.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Otoscopy — examination of the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane

blocks.text: Otoscopy is one of the most important components of the ear examination.

content_groups.group_title: A. How to hold and use the otoscope

blocks.text: Procedure

items.text: Select a clean speculum that fits comfortably into the external auditory canal.
Switch on the light and check that the lens and light source are functioning.
Use your right hand and right eye to examine the patient's right ear.
Use your left hand and left eye to examine the left ear.
Stabilise your hand against the patient's head to reduce the risk of injury if the patient moves suddenly.
In an adult, gently pull the pinna upwards and backwards to straighten the canal.
In a young child, pull the pinna downwards and backwards; the precise technique depends on the child's age and anatomy.
Insert the speculum gently under direct vision, following the canal's direction. Do not force it or advance unnecessarily.
Inspect the canal walls and then the tympanic membrane.
Withdraw the otoscope carefully and repeat on the other side.

blocks.text: The speculum should not be inserted deeply enough to cause pain. If the canal is obstructed by wax, swelling or discharge, do not force the instrument past the obstruction.

content_groups.group_title: B. What to inspect in the external auditory canal

items.text: Patency of the canal.
Amount and appearance of cerumen.
Redness and swelling.
Discharge or debris.
Foreign bodies.
Ulceration or granulation tissue.
Exostoses or bony narrowing.
Fungal debris, if present.

blocks.text: Common findings and their significance

rows: Conductive hearing loss, discomfort or tinnitus
Infection; source may be canal or middle ear
May suggest otomycosis, depending on appearance
May occur in severe infection or cholesteatoma-related disease; requires assessment
May obstruct examination or contribute to hearing problems

blocks.text: Do not diagnose fungal infection from colour alone. Clinical appearance, symptoms and sometimes further examination are needed.
Once the canal is sufficiently clear, inspect the entire visible tympanic membrane.

items.text: Colour and translucency.
Position — normal, retracted or bulging.
Surface and integrity.
Landmarks.
Presence of fluid, air bubbles or other visible abnormalities.
Perforation, scarring or tympanostomy tube.

blocks.text: **Normal tympanic membrane**

blocks.title: A normal tympanic membrane is generally:

items.text: Pearly grey or grey-white.
Translucent.
Intact.
Slightly concave towards the middle ear.
Characterised by visible anatomical landmarks.

blocks.text: The exact appearance varies with age, lighting and individual anatomy.
**Important landmarks**
Handle of the malleus
A prominent landmark extending downwards from the superior part of the membrane towards the umbo. Its position helps orient the examiner.
Umbo
The central point where the tip of the malleus attaches to the tympanic membrane, producing a slight inward depression.
Pars tensa and pars flaccida

The pars tensa forms most of the membrane. The smaller pars flaccida lies superiorly, above the lateral process of the malleus. Retraction pockets, especially in the upper membrane, may be important when assessing for cholesteatoma.
**Cone of light**
A triangular light reflection may be visible from the umbo towards the anteroinferior quadrant:

items.text: Right ear: approximately the 5 o'clock position.
Left ear: approximately the 7 o'clock position.

blocks.text: This is a useful landmark, but its absence alone does not diagnose middle-ear disease.
Bulging tympanic membrane
A bulging membrane with middle-ear effusion and compatible acute symptoms strongly supports acute otitis media. Reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy provides additional evidence of effusion.
Retracted tympanic membrane
May result from negative middle-ear pressure due to Eustachian tube dysfunction. It may be associated with conductive hearing loss or retraction pockets.
Perforation
A visible defect may result from infection, trauma or previous surgery. Describe its site and approximate size, and assess for discharge and associated hearing loss.
Middle-ear effusion
The membrane may look dull, amber or retracted, sometimes with an air-fluid level or bubbles. This can occur in otitis media with effusion.
Retraction pocket or white keratin debris
May indicate cholesteatoma, particularly when located in the attic or upper tympanic membrane. Cholesteatoma can erode bone and damage nearby structures; prompt ENT assessment is important.
Pneumatic otoscopy assesses the mobility of the tympanic membrane by applying a gentle change in air pressure through an appropriate sealed speculum.

items.text: Normal mobility suggests the membrane and middle-ear system can move relatively freely.
Reduced mobility may indicate middle-ear effusion, tympanic membrane scarring or other middle-ear pathology.

blocks.text: This test should only be performed by someone trained to do it, with suitable equipment and after considering the possibility of perforation, trauma or other contraindications. Do not force air into the ear.
Hearing should be assessed in each ear, using a screening method appropriate to the patient.

A patient may have a normal-looking ear and still have significant sensorineural hearing loss. Conversely, visible wax or a perforation does not automatically establish the degree of hearing impairment.
youtube.com
Procedure

items.text: Stand behind or to the side of the patient, approximately 60 cm away, or use the distance specified by your local protocol.
Test one ear at a time.
Mask the non-test ear with gentle rubbing of the tragus or another standardised method, ensuring the patient cannot hear through that ear.
Exhale and whisper a combination of letters and numbers.
Ask the patient to repeat what they heard.
Use different combinations for each ear.
Record the result and repeat or investigate if the response is abnormal.

blocks.text: The exact word combinations and pass criteria vary by protocol.
Limitations: The whisper test is a screening tool. It does not quantify hearing thresholds, and results can be affected by background noise, examiner technique and masking.

A watch or other sound source may be used as an informal screening method by comparing perception at a standardised distance in each ear. It is less standardised than formal audiometry and should not replace it when accurate assessment is needed.
For young children, consider age-appropriate behavioural tests, observation of sound localisation, and formal paediatric audiology when indicated.
A child who does not respond reliably to verbal instructions cannot be assumed to have normal hearing.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Tuning fork tests: Rinne and Weber

blocks.text: These are high-yield OSCE tests used to help distinguish conductive hearing loss (CHL) from sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).
Use a 512 Hz tuning fork for routine bedside hearing assessment. Lower frequencies can be more susceptible to tactile perception and other sources of error.

content_groups.group_title: A. Understand the two types of hearing

blocks.text: Conductive hearing loss
Sound transmission through the external or middle ear is impaired.
Examples include impacted wax, otitis externa with canal obstruction, middle-ear effusion, tympanic membrane perforation and otosclerosis.
Sensorineural hearing loss
Dysfunction affects the cochlea, auditory nerve or associated sensory pathways.
Examples include presbycusis, noise-induced hearing loss, ototoxicity and sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
The Rinne test compares air conduction (AC) with bone conduction (BC) in the same ear.
Procedure

items.text: Strike the tuning fork gently against a suitable soft surface to produce vibration.
Place its base firmly on the mastoid process behind the ear.
Ask the patient to indicate when the sound is no longer heard.
Immediately move the vibrating fork close to the external auditory canal without touching it.
Ask whether the sound is heard again.
Record whether air conduction or bone conduction is perceived as louder or longer.

blocks.text: Avoid striking the fork too forcefully, and ensure the patient understands the instructions.
Interpretation

rows: Normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss

blocks.text: A positive Rinne does not necessarily mean hearing is normal. It can also occur in sensorineural hearing loss.

In severe unilateral sensorineural loss, bone-conducted sound may be heard by the opposite ear, potentially producing a misleading result. Formal audiometry and appropriate masking are important when results are uncertain.
The Weber test compares bone-conducted sound between the two ears.
Procedure

items.text: Strike the tuning fork.
Place its base in the midline of the forehead or vertex.
Ask the patient whether the sound is heard equally in both ears or is louder on one side.
Record the perceived direction of lateralisation.

blocks.text: Interpretation

rows: Sound is usually heard centrally or equally in both ears
Sound tends to lateralise to the affected ear
Sound tends to lateralise to the better-hearing ear

blocks.text: **Clinical interpretation examples**
Example 1: Right conductive hearing loss

items.text: Weber: lateralises to the right.
Right Rinne: negative (BC greater than AC).
Left Rinne: positive.

blocks.text: Interpretation: findings support right conductive hearing loss.
Example 2: Right sensorineural hearing loss

items.text: Weber: lateralises to the left, the better-hearing ear.
Rinne: may remain positive in both ears.

blocks.text: Interpretation: findings support right sensorineural hearing loss, but the degree and type must be confirmed with audiometry.
Example 3: Symmetrical normal hearing

items.text: Weber: central.
Rinne: positive bilaterally.

blocks.text: Interpretation: no clear bedside evidence of asymmetric hearing loss. Mild, symmetrical or high-frequency hearing loss may still be present.
Mnemonic: Weber goes to the bad ear in conductive loss and the good ear in sensorineural loss.
Remember that tuning fork tests are screening tests. They are not substitutes for pure-tone audiometry, especially when hearing loss is sudden, severe or asymmetric.
Formal hearing assessment quantifies the type, degree and configuration of hearing loss.
During pure-tone audiometry, the patient listens to tones of different frequencies and intensities through headphones and, when appropriate, a bone-conduction vibrator.
The patient signals whenever a tone is heard.
Typical frequencies tested range from 250 Hz to 8,000 Hz for air conduction, with bone-conduction testing over a more limited frequency range depending on the equipment and protocol.
Results are plotted on an audiogram, with hearing thresholds recorded in decibels hearing level (dB HL).

rows: Air and bone thresholds are within normal limits
Hearing thresholds are within the expected range
Air conduction is worse than bone conduction, with an air–bone gap
Air and bone thresholds are both reduced without a significant air–bone gap
Air and bone thresholds are reduced, with an air–bone gap

blocks.text: The presence of an air–bone gap must be interpreted alongside masking, test reliability and the full audiogram.
Speech testing assesses the ability to detect and recognise speech. It can help assess functional communication, corroborate pure-tone findings and guide rehabilitation.
Tympanometry measures how the middle-ear system responds to changes in air pressure in the external auditory canal.
It can help assess middle-ear function, including effusion, negative middle-ear pressure and certain abnormalities of the tympanic membrane or ossicular system.

items.text: Type A: a peak near normal pressure, generally consistent with normal middle-ear mechanics.
Type B: a flat trace, which may indicate middle-ear effusion; ear canal volume helps interpretation.
Type C: a peak at negative pressure, suggesting negative middle-ear pressure or Eustachian tube dysfunction.

blocks.text: Tympanometry does not measure hearing thresholds and must be interpreted alongside otoscopy and audiometry.
The vestibular system contributes to balance, spatial orientation and stabilisation of vision during head movement.
A full vestibular examination is not required in every routine ear OSCE. It is particularly relevant when the patient reports vertigo, imbalance, oscillopsia or falls.
Ask the patient to walk normally, turn and return, provided it is safe.

items.text: Unsteadiness.
Broad-based gait.
Veering to one side.
Difficulty turning.
Inability to stand or walk without assistance.

blocks.text: Do not ask a patient with severe vertigo or marked imbalance to perform unsupported balance tests.
Procedure

items.text: Ask the patient to stand with feet together and arms by their sides.
Stand close enough to prevent a fall.
Observe balance with eyes open.
Ask the patient to close their eyes briefly if it is safe to do so.
Observe for increased sway or loss of balance.

blocks.text: A positive Romberg test means balance deteriorates substantially when visual input is removed. This can occur with impaired proprioception or vestibular dysfunction; it is not specific to an inner-ear disorder.
Severe instability even with the eyes open may indicate cerebellar or other neurological dysfunction.
Observe the eyes at rest and, where appropriate, during gaze in different directions.

items.text: Direction: horizontal, vertical or torsional.
Whether it is spontaneous or gaze-evoked.
Whether it changes direction.
Associated vertigo, nausea or neurological symptoms.

blocks.text: Peripheral vestibular disorders commonly produce horizontal-torsional nystagmus, but no single nystagmus pattern independently excludes a central cause.
This tests the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
Procedure

items.text: Explain the manoeuvre and ask the patient to fixate on your nose.
Hold the patient's head gently but firmly.
Make small, rapid, unpredictable rotations of the head to either side.
Observe whether the eyes maintain fixation or make corrective saccades.

blocks.text: A corrective saccade after turning towards one side may indicate reduced vestibular function on that side.

Important limitation: The head impulse test is technically demanding. A normal result does not, by itself, diagnose stroke or exclude a peripheral vestibular disorder. The HINTS examination, which combines head impulse, nystagmus and test of skew, is intended for selected patients with an acute vestibular syndrome and should only be used by clinicians trained in its interpretation. It is not a general screening test for every dizzy patient.
The Dix–Hallpike test is used to assess for posterior-canal BPPV in patients with an appropriate history of brief, position-triggered vertigo.
General procedure

items.text: Explain the manoeuvre and check whether neck or back problems, vascular concerns or mobility limitations make it unsuitable.
Begin with the patient seated.
Turn the head approximately 45 degrees towards the side being tested.
Support the head and lower the patient into a supine position with appropriate neck extension.
Observe the eyes for characteristic positional nystagmus and ask about vertigo.
Return the patient to sitting safely.
Repeat on the other side if indicated.

blocks.text: A positive test for posterior-canal BPPV typically produces a characteristic transient torsional, upbeating nystagmus with the patient's symptoms.

Do not perform the manoeuvre indiscriminately in patients with significant cervical spine limitations or other contraindications. Atypical positional nystagmus, neurological abnormalities or persistent symptoms require further assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Examination of the mastoid, Eustachian tube and surrounding structures

blocks.text: Inspect and palpate both mastoid processes.

items.text: Tenderness.
Redness and swelling.
Fluctuance or a collection.
Loss of the postauricular crease.
Displacement of the pinna.

blocks.text: Mastoiditis is an important complication of middle-ear infection. Postauricular swelling, fever, severe pain and protrusion of the pinna should prompt urgent ENT assessment.
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. It helps equalise middle-ear pressure and drain secretions.

items.text: Ear fullness or pressure.
Popping sensations.
Symptoms during air travel or changes in altitude.
Recent upper respiratory tract infection.
Nasal congestion or allergies.

blocks.text: A history of pressure symptoms together with a retracted tympanic membrane may suggest Eustachian tube dysfunction.

The Valsalva manoeuvre may sometimes be used to assess pressure equalisation, but it is not a definitive diagnostic test. It should not be forced, particularly where acute infection, significant pain or relevant contraindications exist.

content_groups.group_title: C. Examine the nose and throat

blocks.text: The ear examination may need to extend to the upper respiratory tract because the middle ear communicates with the nasopharynx through the Eustachian tube.

items.text: Nasal cavity for congestion, discharge or obstruction.
Oral cavity and oropharynx.
Tonsils and posterior pharynx.
Temporomandibular joints.
Dentition, when referred otalgia is suspected.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult, particularly without a clear explanation, warrants ENT assessment of the nasopharynx to exclude an obstructing lesion.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Cranial nerve examination relevant to the ear

blocks.text: Ear disease can affect structures close to several cranial nerves. A focused neurological examination is especially important when there is facial weakness, vertigo, hearing loss or a suspected complication of infection.

rows: Facial sensation and jaw movement when indicated
Raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly, smile and puff out cheeks
Hearing tests, vestibular assessment when indicated
Voice quality, palate and swallowing when indicated
Shoulder shrug and head rotation when indicated
Tongue protrusion and movement when indicated

blocks.text: The facial nerve passes through the temporal bone, making it relevant to ear disease and trauma.

items.text: Raise both eyebrows.
Close their eyes tightly against resistance.
Smile and show their teeth.
Puff out their cheeks.

blocks.text: New facial weakness associated with ear pain, vesicular lesions around the ear or acute otitis media requires urgent assessment. Facial weakness following trauma also raises concern for temporal bone injury.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Common ear conditions: examination findings and interpretation

blocks.text: Otitis externa

items.text: Ear pain, often worsened by touching the tragus or moving the pinna.
Canal erythema and oedema.
Possible discharge.
Hearing may be reduced if the canal is obstructed.

blocks.text: Acute otitis media

items.text: Ear pain, sometimes with fever or preceding respiratory infection.
Bulging tympanic membrane and middle-ear effusion.
Reduced membrane mobility when assessed appropriately.
A perforation may develop, sometimes with discharge.

blocks.text: Otitis media with effusion

items.text: Middle-ear fluid without the acute inflammatory features of acute otitis media.
Dull or amber membrane, possible air-fluid level.
Reduced membrane mobility.
Often associated with conductive hearing loss.

blocks.text: Cholesteatoma

items.text: May cause persistent, foul-smelling discharge and hearing loss.
An attic retraction pocket or keratin debris may be visible.
May erode the ossicles or surrounding bone.
Requires ENT assessment.

blocks.text: Otosclerosis

items.text: Progressive conductive hearing loss is typical.
The tympanic membrane is often normal.
Diagnosis relies on audiometry and specialist assessment.

blocks.text: These findings should change the urgency of your management.

rows: Sudden hearing loss over hours to a few days
Possible sudden sensorineural hearing loss; urgent ENT assessment is required
Postauricular swelling with fever and ear pain
Severe ear pain in a patient with diabetes or immunosuppression
Possible facial nerve involvement or serious infection
Clear fluid or blood from the ear after head trauma
Possible temporal bone injury or cerebrospinal fluid leak
Foreign body consisting of a button battery
Time-critical tissue injury; urgent removal by an appropriately equipped clinician
Painful red ear after cartilage piercing
Persistent unilateral discharge, granulation tissue or suspected cholesteatoma
Possible destructive or chronic ear disease
Vertigo with focal neurological signs or inability to walk
Possible central neurological pathology, including stroke

blocks.text: Do not attempt blind removal of a button battery, irrigate an ear containing a suspected battery, or delay urgent referral while attempting routine examination.
A reliable sequence helps prevent omissions under examination pressure.

items.text: Preparation: Introduce yourself, obtain consent and ask about pain.
Inspection: Examine both pinnae and the surrounding skin.
Palpation: Check the tragus, pinna and mastoid region.
Otoscopy: Inspect the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane on both sides.
Hearing screening: Perform a whispered voice test or another appropriate screening test.
Tuning fork tests: Perform Weber and Rinne when hearing loss is suspected or the OSCE requires them.
Vestibular assessment: Examine gait, balance, nystagmus and perform selected manoeuvres if indicated.
Extended examination: Assess cranial nerves, nose, throat and temporomandibular joint when clinically appropriate.
Completion: Thank the patient, explain findings and discuss further tests or referral.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. How to present your findings to the examiner

blocks.text: **Ear Examination — Sample Normal Findings**

Both pinnae were symmetrical, with no visible deformity, swelling, skin lesions or discharge. There was no tenderness on manipulation of either pinna or tragus, and no mastoid tenderness or postauricular swelling.

Otoscopy showed patent external auditory canals without significant erythema, oedema, discharge or obstructing cerumen. Both tympanic membranes were intact, pearly grey and translucent, with identifiable landmarks and no obvious bulging, retraction or perforation.
Hearing was symmetrical on bedside screening. Weber testing did not lateralise, and Rinne testing was positive bilaterally, with air conduction greater than bone conduction.
There was no obvious nystagmus or gait abnormality on the components of vestibular examination performed. Relevant cranial nerve examination revealed no obvious abnormality.
**Conclusion:** No obvious abnormality was detected on the components of the ear examination performed.

Only report the tests you actually performed. For example, do not document normal tuning fork results if you did not perform Rinne and Weber, and do not claim that the tympanic membranes were normal if cerumen prevented adequate visualisation.
Introduce yourself, obtain consent and take a focused ear history
Inspect both pinnae, external auditory meatuses and surrounding skin
Palpate the tragus, pinna and mastoid processes
Perform otoscopy on both ears using the correct technique
Inspect the external canal for wax, inflammation, discharge and foreign bodies
Inspect the tympanic membrane for colour, position, landmarks and integrity
Perform whispered voice hearing screening
Perform Weber test when indicated
Perform Rinne test when indicated
Interpret conductive versus sensorineural hearing loss
Assess gait, balance and nystagmus if indicated
Perform selected vestibular manoeuvres safely when indicated
Assess facial nerve function and other cranial nerves when relevant
Examine the nose, throat or temporomandibular joint when indicated
Identify emergencies and state appropriate referral
Present the findings clearly and systematically
Reset checklist
**High-yield facts to memorise**

items.text: Adult: pull the pinna upwards and backwards during otoscopy; in young children, generally downwards and backwards.
Rinne positive: air conduction is greater than bone conduction; this occurs in normal hearing and sensorineural hearing loss.
Rinne negative: bone conduction is greater than air conduction; this suggests conductive hearing loss.
Weber: sound generally lateralises to the affected ear in unilateral conductive loss and to the better ear in unilateral sensorineural loss.
Otitis externa: tragal tenderness and canal inflammation are characteristic.
Acute otitis media: a bulging tympanic membrane with compatible acute symptoms is a key finding.
Cholesteatoma: suspect it with characteristic retraction pockets, keratin debris and persistent foul-smelling discharge.
Mastoiditis: postauricular swelling and tenderness with displacement of the pinna require urgent assessment.
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: do not delay urgent referral for routine wax removal or further bedside testing.

blocks.text: The most important principle is to combine the history, otoscopic findings, hearing assessment and neurological examination. No single finding—including a normal-looking tympanic membrane or normal tuning fork test—can exclude every clinically significant ear disorder.
